study.title: 1 Timothy 1 Correction of the doctrine, the use of the law and discipline in the church
study.overview: This chapter opens Paul's letter to Timothy with a combination of apostolic authority, pastoral care and direct confrontation with doctrinal errors. Paul recalls that his mission comes from God and Christ, calls Timothy to remain in Ephesus to correct false teachings and shows that the purpose of God's instruction is not speculation, but love, clean conscience, and sincere faith. He then explains the value of the law when used correctly: it exposes sin and addresses those who live in rebellion against sound doctrine. Paul then interrupts the exhortation to thank for the mercy received, for his own conversion and called to the ministry illustrate Christ's patience with sinners. The chapter ends with a final charge to Timothy and the disciplinary mention of Himenaeus and Alexander, who rejected the faith and began to blaspheme.

outline.title: Apostolic greeting and bond with Timothy
outline.explanation: Paul presents himself as an apostle by order of God and Christ, and greets Timothy as a true son in the faith, asking for grace, mercy and peace. The opening establishes authority and pastoral affection at the same time.

outline.title: Order to combat strange doctrines
outline.explanation: Timothy must remain in Ephesus to prevent different teachings from the gospel, distancing the church from endless myths and genealogies. The target of divine instruction is not dispute, but love that is born of pure heart, good consciousness and faith without pretending.

outline.title: Misuse of the law and sound doctrine
outline.explanation: Some have deviated from the purpose of faith and want to teach the law without understanding it. Paul states that the law is good when used legitimately, for it denounces those who live in rebellion, in moral sins and in practices contrary to sound doctrine, all this in contrast to the glorious gospel entrusted to the apostle.

outline.title: Mercy received, doxology and final discipline
outline.explanation: Paul thanks for Christ for strengthening him and put him in the ministry, though he was blasphemous and persecutor. His history becomes an example of Christ's patience with sinners, culminates in worship of the one God, and ends with a new charge to Timothy, in addition to the mention of Himenaeus and Alexander, who wrecked in faith and were given to discipline to learn not to blaspheme.

study.context: The chapter shows that Timothy was in Ephesus as Paul's representative, in charge of facing people who promoted another teaching. The text does not detail the external scenario much, but it makes it clear that there was doctrinal conflict within the community and the need for pastoral correction. It also appears a strong awareness of ministry as a so-called received, not as human initiative.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter unites truth and piety. The right doctrine must produce love, inner purity, right consciousness and genuine faith; without this, teaching becomes empty debate. The law is not denied, but placed in its proper use: it exposes sin and shows the necessity of grace. The gospel appears as a proclamation of salvation for sinners, centered on the mercy and patience of Christ. Paul's experience works as a living proof that no one is out of reach of grace. Finally, discipline against those who persist in blasphemy shows that the church must protect the faith received and take doctrinal sin seriously.

scholarViews.insight: The opening follows the pattern of an ancient letter, but with additions that reinforce the authority of Paul's message; this clearly appears in the initial greeting, where the apostle writes in the name of God and Christ.
The end of the commandment is love; for Matthew Henry, God's law seeks to produce love for God and others, and any teaching that weakens that love frustrates the purpose of the commandment.

Delivering Himenaeus and Alexander to Satan means submitting them to severe discipline, for the destruction of the flesh and correction of their sin of blasphemy, and not simply to abandon the hope of restoration.

questions: Does my way of learning and teaching the Bible produce love, purity and sincere faith, or just intellectual discussions and vanity?
How did I use the law of God: to accuse others, or to recognize my own sin and lead me to the gospel?
Is the discipline of the church, when necessary, seen by me as an expression of holy zeal and corrective care, or just as punishment?
study.practice: Choose a concrete practice for this week: to reject a source of teaching that feeds empty disputes, to separate daily a time to examine one's conscience before God, and pray for someone who is away from faith so that Christ's mercy will reach it again. If you exercise Christian leadership, treat doctrinal correction with firmness and meekness, always aiming at restoration and fidelity to the gospel.
study.uncertainty: The text and notes do not identify with certainty the date, the exact situation of the church in Ephesus, nor the specific position of Himeneu and Alexander; the disciplinary application described in the grades is interpretative and may vary in detail between translators and commentators. There are also differences of nuance in the phrase lists of verse 10 between translations, and the term translated here as a sexual practice between men reflects the writing provided in the presented biblical text.
